newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-INTERVIEW-Swiss gold sales plan misread - WGC.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-INTERVIEW-Swiss gold sales plan misread - WGC.

text.p: The World Gold Council on Thursday said the market had overreacted to news of planned changes in gold holdings by the Swiss National Bank (SNB).

April COMEX gold dived to an eight-day low of US$352.50 on Wednesday before ending the day down US$6.10 at US$354.50 an ounce on concerns the Swiss central bank planned to unload up to 400 tonnes of gold over 10 years.
However, WGC gold market analyst George Milling-Stanley told Reuters the market has misread the bank's intentions.
Swiss President Arnold Koller proposed on Wednesday that a memorial foundation be established for victims of the Holocaust and other tragedies.
Its capital fund of about seven billion Swiss francs would be raised through selling revalued Swiss gold reserves.
This would entail selling gold over a 10-year period, SNB chairman Hans Meyer said.
Some analysts translated that as meaning Switzerland would sell about 40 tonnes of gold a year to capitalise the fund.
SNB's gold reserves of 2,600 tonnes are valued at the fixed legal parity of 4,595.74 francs per kg.
"The Swiss government has said it is considering re-valuing its offical reserves at something closer to the market price," Milling-Stanley said in a statement.
"They are currently on the books at US$112-$118 an ounce, way lower than the market price" he said.
Milling-Stanley said some banks value their reserves at as low as US$42 an ounce.

But the Swiss are considering revaluing the gold up somewhere closer to the market price and maybe using some of the book proceeds from that transaction to set up an additional fund to help victims and survivors from the Holocaust, he said.
"The market's got this all out of proportion and that's why the market is down six bucks," Milling-Stanley told Reuters. "People have suddenly decided the Swiss bank is going to sell."
He said the SNB has made it clear it was not contemplating sales of gold but rather a book revaluation of reserves.
"It's not been said they are considering selling," he said.
The possibility of the Swiss revaluing their gold reserves closer to market prices has come up in line with ways of generating greater yields on their holdings, including gold, Milling-Stanley said.
The likelihood was not that the SNB will sell gold but that it will probably get involved in the gold deposit market in leasing the metal, Milling-Stanley said.

"Gold costs money to store, but if you lend it out to the market, you save security and insurance costs and the borrower is prepared to pay a return which is currently in excess of the return on the yen or deutschemark deposits," he said.
"Suddenly gold is up there as one of the better profit earners among central bank reserves instead of something that is regarded as a sterile, non-yielding asset," he said.
"What the Swiss have done traditionally is put a valuation on gold is way below any current market price to avoid valuing it back down if the price was to come off," he said.
He said the current valuation was conservative, which is not unusual for a central bank.

"A lot of banks value gold at acquisition costs, which for many central banks is US$42 an ounce from when it was fixed, or even US$35 in the earlier period of the price being fixed," Milling-Stanley said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
